Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Current: by its nature readily realisable AND intended to be held for not more than one year from the date it is made. Long-term: everything else.

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: How are current investments measured under AS 13?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Lower of cost and fair value — current investments measured at the lower of acquisition cost and fair value/market value (AS 13).

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: How are long‑term investments carried and when is a provision required?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: At cost — long‑term investments carried at cost; provide only for diminution that is other‑than‑temporary (AS 13).

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: If a market decline is temporary, what does AS 13 require?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: No provision — temporary declines in market value are not provided for; only other‑than‑temporary declines require provision (AS 13).

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: How should recovery after an earlier 'other‑than‑temporary' provision be accounted?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Up to prior provision — recovery reverses only the earlier provision and is credited to profit & loss to that extent (AS 13).

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: Which acquisition costs are included in 'cost of investment' under AS 13?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Inclusive — cost comprises purchase price plus directly attributable acquisition costs (brokerage, fees, stamp duty) (AS 13).

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: Bonus shares and rights shares on an investment — cost treatment?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Bonus: NO cost added; quantity rises, so cost per share falls. Rights subscribed: price paid is added to carrying amount. Rights sold: proceeds to P&L — unless bought cum-right and ex-right market value is below cost, then reduce the carrying amount.

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: Reclassification between long-term and current — at what value?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Long-term → current: lower of COST and CARRYING AMOUNT on the transfer date. Current → long-term: lower of COST and FAIR VALUE on the transfer date.

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: Where are gains or losses on sale of investments shown?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Profit/Loss in P&L — gains or losses on sale of both current and long‑term investments are recognised in the statement of profit and loss (AS 13).

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: What investment disclosures are mandatory under AS 13?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Disclose — classification (current/long‑term), cost, market/fair value of quoted investments, aggregate provision for diminution and particulars by category (AS 13).

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: Bought cum-interest — how is the price split in the investment account?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Accrued interest from the last interest date to the purchase date is NOT cost: debit it to the interest column. Only the balance is capital cost. On sale, split the proceeds the same way.

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: Current investments — compare cost and fair value at what level?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Individually, or category-wise (equity, preference, debentures) — never on an overall/global basis. Long-term investments are assessed individually.

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: Dividend received out of pre-acquisition profits?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: It is a recovery of cost — credit the investment (reduce carrying amount), not income. Only the post-acquisition part is income.

Investment Accounts (AS 13).front: Selling part of a holding — which cost is matched?
Investment Accounts (AS 13).back: Average carrying amount of the total holding (weighted average cost). Profit = net sale proceeds (after brokerage) minus that average cost.
Land or building not intended to be occupied substantially for own use or operations. Accounted as a LONG-TERM investment: cost less other-than-temporary diminution.

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: What is the maturity limit for 'cash equivalents' under AS 3?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: 3 months — cash equivalents are short‑term, highly liquid investments convertible to known amounts of cash with original maturities of three months or less. (AS 3)

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: Which activity categories must be shown separately in the cash flow statement?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: 3 classes — operating, investing and financing activities must be separately disclosed. (AS 3)

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: Which methods are permitted for reporting operating cash flows and which requires reconciliation to profit?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: 2 methods — Direct or Indirect; Indirect reconciles net profit to net cash from operating activities by adjusting non‑cash items and working capital. (AS 3)

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: Bank overdraft in an AS 3 cash flow statement?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: AS 3 is silent. Treat it as a borrowing — financing activity — and say so in a note. The 'part of cash equivalents if integral to cash management' rule is Ind AS 7, not this syllabus.

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: Interest and dividends — classification under AS 3?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: Non-financial enterprise: interest PAID and dividend PAID = financing; interest and dividend RECEIVED = investing. Financial enterprise: interest paid and interest/dividend received = operating. Dividend paid is always financing. No free choice.

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: Where are income taxes paid presented in the cash flow statement?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: Operating — income taxes paid are cash flows from operating activities unless they can be specifically identified with investing or financing activities. (AS 3)

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: How are non‑cash investing and financing transactions treated in AS 3?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: 0 cash — non‑cash investing and financing transactions are excluded from the cash flow statement and must be disclosed separately in the notes. (AS 3)

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: When preparing the indirect method, which adjustments reconcile profit to cash from operations?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: 3 adjustments — add back non‑cash expenses (deprn, provns), remove non‑cash incomes, and adjust for gains/losses and working‑capital movements. (AS 3)

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: How are proceeds from issue or repayment of borrowings classified?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: Financing — proceeds from issue and repayments of borrowings, and movements in share capital, are cash flows from financing activities. (AS 3)

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: How are purchases and sales of fixed assets and investments shown in the CFS?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: Investing — cash paid to acquire, and cash received on disposal of, fixed assets and investments are classified as investing activities. (AS 3)

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: What must be disclosed about cash balances that are not available for use?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: Material restrictions — disclose cash and cash equivalents not available for use by the entity and explain the nature of restrictions. (AS 3)

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: Proposed dividend in a cash flow question — what was actually paid?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: LAST year's proposed dividend is this year's cash outflow (paid after the AGM). This year's proposed dividend is not a liability (AS 4) and not a cash flow. Add any interim dividend paid this year.

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: Extraordinary items in the cash flow statement?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: Classify as operating, investing or financing as appropriate and disclose SEPARATELY — e.g. insurance claim for earthquake loss of stock = operating; of a building = investing.

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: Foreign currency cash flows and unrealised exchange gains?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: Record at the rate on the date of the cash flow. Unrealised exchange differences are not cash flows; the effect on cash held in foreign currency is shown separately to reconcile opening and closing cash.

Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).front: Acquisition or disposal of a subsidiary — presentation?
Cash Flow Statement (AS 3).back: A separate line under INVESTING activities, net of cash and cash equivalents acquired or disposed of.

Buyback of Shares.front: State the maximum aggregate limit for buyback in a financial year under Companies Act s.68.
Buyback of Shares.back: 25% — buyback in a financial year shall not exceed 25% of the aggregate of paid‑up capital and free reserves (s.68).

Buyback of Shares.front: Limit on the NUMBER of equity shares bought back in a year?
Buyback of Shares.back: Not more than 25% of the total paid-up equity capital of that financial year — the 'shares outstanding test'. Applies alongside the 25%-of-capital-and-free-reserves 'resources test'.

Buyback of Shares.front: What is the maximum permissible debt‑to‑equity ratio after a buyback?
Buyback of Shares.back: 2:1 — the company’s post‑buyback debt‑equity ratio must not exceed 2:1 (s.68).

Buyback of Shares.front: Up to what percentage can the board alone approve a buyback without shareholder special resolution?
Buyback of Shares.back: 10% — board resolution may authorise buyback up to 10% of aggregate paid‑up capital and free reserves; beyond that a special resolution is required (s.68/Buy‑back Rules).

No new buyback offer within 1 year of closing the previous one. No fresh issue of the same kind of shares for 6 months after — except bonus shares and conversions (warrants, ESOPs, sweat equity, preference shares, debentures). Complete within 1 year of the resolution.

Buyback of Shares.front: Out of which funds can a buyback be made (s.68(1))?
Buyback of Shares.back: Free reserves, securities premium account, or proceeds of an issue of shares or other specified securities — but NOT the proceeds of an earlier issue of the SAME kind of shares.

Default in repaying deposits or interest, redeeming debentures or preference shares, paying dividend, or repaying a term loan or interest to a bank/FI — unless remedied and 3 years have passed. Also: not through a subsidiary or investment company.
From existing holders on a proportionate basis (tender offer); from the open market; from employees holding ESOP or sweat equity securities.

Buyback of Shares.front: Within how many days must shares bought back be extinguished and records updated after completion?
Buyback of Shares.back: 7 days — bought‑back shares must be extinguished, share certificates cancelled and statutory registers updated within 7 days of completion (Buy‑back Rules).

Buyback of Shares.front: What statutory filings and time limits must follow a buyback (special resolution route)?
Buyback of Shares.back: 30 days — file MGT‑14 within 30 days of passing special resolution; file return of buyback (Form SH‑11) with ROC within 30 days of completion (Companies Act/Buy‑back Rules).

Buyback of Shares.front: The three tests for maximum buyback — and which one wins?
Buyback of Shares.back: 1) Shares outstanding: 25% of equity shares. 2) Resources: 25% of paid-up capital + free reserves ÷ buyback price. 3) Debt-equity: post-buyback debt not more than twice capital + free reserves. Answer = the LOWEST of the three.

Buyback of Shares.front: Debt-equity test — how is the maximum buyback worked out?
Buyback of Shares.back: Minimum equity to keep = total debt ÷ 2. Let x = transfer to CRR and y = buyback amount: (shareholders' funds − x) − y = minimum equity, and y = (x ÷ face value) × buyback price. Solve the two together — CRR is not a free reserve.

Buyback of Shares.front: Journal treatment of the premium paid and the CRR on buyback?
Buyback of Shares.back: Premium on buyback: debit Securities Premium / free reserves. CRR (s.69): transfer the NOMINAL value of shares bought back out of free reserves or securities premium. No CRR for the part funded by a fresh issue.

Declaration of solvency SH-9 before the buyback; letter of offer SH-8; special resolution in MGT-14 within 30 days; extinguish shares within 7 days of completion; return of buyback SH-11 within 30 days of completion; register in SH-10.

Company Final Accounts.front: When is an asset or liability classified as 'current' under Schedule III — what time test do you apply?
Company Final Accounts.back: 12 months — amounts expected to be realized/settled within 12 months from the reporting date are current; otherwise non‑current (Schedule III, Companies Act, classification rule).

Company Final Accounts.front: Order of headings in the Schedule III (Division I) balance sheet?
Company Final Accounts.back: Equity & Liabilities: (1) Shareholders' funds; (2) Share application money pending allotment; (3) Non-current liabilities; (4) Current liabilities. Assets: (1) Non-current assets; (2) Current assets.

Company Final Accounts.front: Instalments of a long-term loan due within 12 months — where shown?
Company Final Accounts.back: Under SHORT-TERM BORROWINGS as 'current maturities of long-term borrowings' (2021 amendment — earlier it sat in Other current liabilities).
Overall 11% of net profits (computed u/s 198). One MD/WTD/manager: 5%; more than one: 10% in all. Other directors: 1% if there is an MD/WTD/manager, otherwise 3%. Sitting fees are outside the limit.

Company Final Accounts.front: Exceptional vs extraordinary items in the Division I Statement of P&L?
Company Final Accounts.back: BOTH have their own line. Exceptional items: shown before 'profit before extraordinary items and tax'. Extraordinary items: shown separately after that (AS 5). The 'no extraordinary items' rule is Ind AS.

Company Final Accounts.front: How must prior‑period items be shown in company financial statements?
Company Final Accounts.back: Separate disclosure — Prior‑period items must be shown separately in the Statement of Profit & Loss and explained in notes (AS 5, Accounting Standards).

Company Final Accounts.front: When must deferred tax be recognised — and does a revaluation surplus attract deferred tax?
Company Final Accounts.back: Timing differences only — recognise deferred tax for timing differences (AS 22); do NOT recognise deferred tax on a revaluation surplus (AS 22).

Company Final Accounts.front: If a company's operating cycle cannot be readily identified, what period do you use to classify current assets/liabilities?
Company Final Accounts.back: 12 months default — when operating cycle is indeterminate, use 12 months as the operating cycle for classifying current assets and liabilities (Schedule III practice).

Company Final Accounts.front: What are the recognition rules for a provision versus a contingent liability under company accounts?
Company Final Accounts.back: Probable outflow — recognise a provision when a present obligation exists and probable outflow of resources is expected; contingent liabilities are disclosed, not recognised (AS 29: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities).

Company Final Accounts.front: Shareholding disclosures in the share capital note?
Company Final Accounts.back: Each shareholder holding MORE THAN 5% of shares (name, number, %); shares held by the holding company and its group; promoters' shareholding with % change during the year; reconciliation of opening and closing number of shares.

Company Final Accounts.front: Where are 'exceptional items' shown in the Statement of Profit & Loss and how must they be explained?
Company Final Accounts.back: Before tax — exceptional items are shown separately (as 'Exceptional items') affecting profit before tax; disclose nature and amount in notes (Schedule III).

Company Final Accounts.front: Rounding off in Schedule III — the rule after the 2021 amendment?
Company Final Accounts.back: Now mandatory, based on TOTAL INCOME: below ₹100 crore — nearest hundreds, thousands, lakhs or millions; ₹100 crore or more — nearest lakhs, millions or crores. One unit used uniformly.

Company Final Accounts.front: Debit balance of P&L, calls in arrears, forfeited shares — where do they go?
Company Final Accounts.back: Debit P&L balance: a NEGATIVE figure under 'Surplus' in Reserves & Surplus (even if the total turns negative). Calls unpaid: deducted from subscribed capital. Forfeited shares amount: added to share capital.

Company Final Accounts.front: Proposed final dividend at year-end — provide or disclose?
Company Final Accounts.back: Disclose in the NOTES only. Dividend declared after the balance sheet date is not a liability at that date (AS 4, revised). It is adjusted in Surplus in the year it is paid.

Company Final Accounts.front: New disclosures added to Schedule III in 2021 — the ones to name?
Company Final Accounts.back: Ageing schedules for trade receivables and trade payables; ageing of CWIP and intangibles under development; promoters' shareholding; key ratios with explanation for change above 25%; security deposits under Other non-current assets.

Amalgamation.front: Name the two types of amalgamation under AS 14 and the accounting method each uses.
Amalgamation.back: Amalgamation in the nature of merger — pooling of interests (book values); Amalgamation in the nature of purchase — purchase method (assets/liabilities at fair value; goodwill/capital reserve). [AS 14]

Amalgamation.front: The five conditions for 'amalgamation in the nature of merger' (AS 14)?
Amalgamation.back: 1) ALL assets and liabilities taken over. 2) Holders of at least 90% of the face value of equity become equity holders of the transferee. 3) Consideration to them wholly in equity shares (cash only for fractions). 4) Business intended to be carried on. 5) Book values unchanged, except to align accounting policies.

Amalgamation.front: How are assets and liabilities recorded under the purchase method on amalgamation?
Amalgamation.back: At their fair (revalued) values as at the date of amalgamation; differences with consideration produce goodwill or capital reserve. [AS 14]

Amalgamation.front: State the rule to decide Goodwill versus Capital Reserve on amalgamation.
Amalgamation.back: If Purchase Consideration > Net Assets at fair value → Goodwill; if Purchase Consideration < Net Assets at fair value → Capital Reserve (surplus). [AS 14]

Amalgamation.front: What is the treatment of investments and inter-company balances on amalgamation?
Amalgamation.back: All inter-company investments and balances between transferor and transferee are eliminated/cancelled on amalgamation. [AS 14]

Amalgamation.front: How are the reserves of the transferor treated in a merger in the nature of merger?
Amalgamation.back: All reserves (capital and revenue) of the transferor are carried forward in the transferee’s books at their existing carrying amounts. [AS 14]

Amalgamation.front: Give the concise stepwise order to account under the purchase method (most-committed exam step sequence).
Amalgamation.back: 6-step order: (1) Determine purchase consideration, (2) Revalue assets/liabilities at fair value, (3) Eliminate investments/intercompany balances, (4) Compute net assets at fair value, (5) Goodwill/Capital Reserve = consideration − net assets, (6) Pass entries. [AS 14]

Amalgamation.front: How is the share-exchange ratio reflected in accounting for a merger in the nature of merger?
Amalgamation.back: Use the agreed exchange ratio to record equity issued at nominal value in transferee; share capital of transferor is cancelled and differences adjust reserves. [AS 14]

Amalgamation.front: Purchase consideration — what is in and what is out?
Amalgamation.back: Only what is paid to the SHAREHOLDERS (equity and preference) of the transferor — shares, cash, other assets. Payments to debenture holders and creditors, and liquidation expenses, are NOT consideration.

Amalgamation.front: Liquidation expenses of the transferor — treatment?
Amalgamation.back: Borne by transferor: debit Realisation A/c. Borne by transferee: debit Goodwill / Capital Reserve (purchase method) or General Reserve / P&L (merger). Never part of purchase consideration.

Amalgamation.front: Statutory reserves of the transferor under the PURCHASE method?
Amalgamation.back: Must still be carried: debit Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve, credit the Statutory Reserve. Reverse the entry when the reserve is no longer required. Other reserves of the transferor disappear.

Amalgamation.front: Which Companies Act provisions govern merger/amalgamation approvals and tribunal jurisdiction?
Amalgamation.back: Companies Act, 2013 — Sections 230–232 cover compromise/arrangement and merger/amalgamation; scheme requires NCLT approval and compliance with statutory procedure.
Over its useful life, not exceeding FIVE years unless a somewhat longer period can be justified (AS 14).

Amalgamation.front: Pooling of interests — share capital issued differs from the transferor's capital?
Amalgamation.back: The difference is adjusted in RESERVES of the transferee. No goodwill or capital reserve arises under the merger method.

Amalgamation.front: Inter-company stock containing unrealised profit on amalgamation?
Amalgamation.back: Cancel mutual debtors/creditors and bills. Unrealised profit in stock: reduce the stock and debit Goodwill / Capital Reserve (purchase) or General Reserve (merger).

Amalgamation.front: Net payment method vs net assets method for consideration?
Amalgamation.back: Net payment: add up everything paid to shareholders in each form. Net assets: agreed value of assets taken over minus liabilities taken over. If the question gives the payments, net payment prevails.

Internal Reconstruction.front: Which Companies Act provisions commonly govern an internal reconstruction scheme?
Internal Reconstruction.back: Sections 230–234 (compromise, arrangement & reconstruction) and Section 66 (reduction of share capital). Schemes need NCLT sanction and compliance with the Companies (Compromises etc.) rules.

Internal Reconstruction.front: Which authority must sanction an internal reconstruction before it is effective?
Internal Reconstruction.back: NCLT order is required (under ss.230/66); scheme becomes binding only after the Tribunal's sanction and statutory filings.

Internal Reconstruction.front: State the fundamental accounting difference between internal reconstruction and external reconstruction (amalgamation).
Internal Reconstruction.back: 1 company survives after internal reconstruction; assets/liabilities remain with same legal entity. External reconstruction (amalgamation) transfers assets/liabilities to another/new company (apply AS 14).

Internal Reconstruction.front: What exact sequence of accounting steps should you follow to prepare a reconstructed balance sheet (exam sequence)?
Internal Reconstruction.back: 1) Record agreed asset/liability valuations; 2) Write off fictitious assets and P&L debit via Reconstruction A/c; 3) Adjust share-capital (cancel/surrender & reissue); 4) Close Reconstruction A/c; 5) Prepare reconstructed balance sheet.

Internal Reconstruction.front: How are fictitious assets dealt with in internal reconstruction accounts?
Internal Reconstruction.back: All fictitious assets must be written off — transferred to Reconstruction A/c and fully written off (cannot appear in reconstructed balance sheet).

Internal Reconstruction.front: How is the debit balance of Profit & Loss account treated in internal reconstruction?
Internal Reconstruction.back: Debit balance of P&L is written off via Reconstruction A/c against distributable reserves first (if permitted) and thereafter absorbed by capital reduction as per the sanctioned scheme.

Internal Reconstruction.front: Reconstruction (Capital Reduction) Account — nature and how it is closed?
Internal Reconstruction.back: A temporary account: credited with sacrifices by shareholders and creditors and appreciation in assets; debited with losses, fictitious assets and write-downs. Any credit balance left goes to CAPITAL RESERVE.

Internal Reconstruction.front: Entry for reducing a ₹10 share to ₹6 fully paid?
Internal Reconstruction.back: Equity Share Capital (₹10) A/c Dr 10 → To Equity Share Capital (₹6) A/c 6, To Capital Reduction A/c 4. The sacrifice is the credit to Capital Reduction.

Internal Reconstruction.front: How must unrecorded assets or liabilities discovered during reconstruction be treated in accounting?
Internal Reconstruction.back: Any unrecorded assets/liabilities are recognised at agreed values; resultant gain/loss is taken to Reconstruction A/c and treated according to the sanctioned scheme.

Internal Reconstruction.front: Alteration of capital u/s 61 vs reduction u/s 66?
Internal Reconstruction.back: s.61 (increase, consolidation, sub-division, conversion to stock, cancel unissued): ordinary resolution if articles permit; Tribunal only if consolidation changes voting percentages. s.66 reduction: special resolution + Tribunal confirmation.

Internal Reconstruction.front: Arrears of preference dividend waived or settled in a reconstruction?
Internal Reconstruction.back: Arrears are only a contingent liability — no entry for the part WAIVED. Any amount actually paid or settled in shares is debited to Capital Reduction A/c.

Internal Reconstruction.front: Creditors or debenture holders agree to a cut — entry?
Internal Reconstruction.back: Creditors / Debentures A/c Dr → To Capital Reduction A/c with the amount sacrificed. If they take new shares or debentures in settlement, credit those for the agreed value.

Consolidation.front: When is an enterprise a subsidiary under AS 21?
Consolidation.back: Control = ownership, directly or through subsidiaries, of MORE THAN ONE-HALF of the voting power, OR control of the composition of the board of directors so as to obtain economic benefits.

Consolidation.front: How is minority interest measured under AS 21?
Consolidation.back: Minority's % of the subsidiary's net assets: their share of equity at the date of acquisition plus their share of movements since. Shown separately from liabilities and the parent's equity. No fair-value option.

Consolidation.front: Goodwill or capital reserve on consolidation — the formula?
Consolidation.back: Cost of investment minus parent's share of the subsidiary's equity on the acquisition date (capital + pre-acquisition reserves). Positive = GOODWILL. Negative = CAPITAL RESERVE (never a gain in P&L).

Consolidation.front: How are pre‑acquisition and post‑acquisition profits of a subsidiary treated on consolidation?
Consolidation.back: Pre/post: Pre‑acq profits are part of net assets at acquisition and reduce goodwill; post‑acq profits included in consolidated profit and apportioned between parent and minority interest (AS 21).

Consolidation.front: Unrealised profit in unsold intra-group stock?
Consolidation.back: Eliminate IN FULL. Downstream (parent sold): all borne by the group. Upstream (subsidiary sold): reduce the subsidiary's profit, so the minority bears its share.

Consolidation.front: How to treat intra‑group transfer of a depreciable fixed asset that remains in transferee's books?
Consolidation.back: Eliminate: Remove unrealised gain from asset carrying amount and reverse excess depreciation since transfer; adjust current depreciation and split effect with minority interest (AS 21).

Consolidation.front: How are dividends received from a subsidiary treated for consolidation when declared out of pre‑ and post‑acquisition profits?
Consolidation.back: Dividend from pre‑acq profits reduces cost of investment; dividend from post‑acq profits recognised as income and apportioned between parent and minority interest (AS 21).

Consolidation.front: What percentage presumes 'significant influence' and how are associates accounted (AS 23)?
Consolidation.back: 20%: Holding of 20% or more of voting power presumes significant influence; associates are accounted for by the equity method (AS 23).

Consolidation.front: Parent and subsidiary have different reporting dates (AS 21)?
Consolidation.back: Allowed if the gap is not more than SIX months; adjust for significant transactions in between. (Three months is the Ind AS 110 figure.)

Consolidation.front: Cost of investment is LESS than the parent's share of equity — treatment?
Consolidation.back: Capital Reserve on consolidation, shown in the consolidated balance sheet. AS 21 has no 'bargain purchase gain' in P&L.

Consolidation.front: Give the correct sequence of core consolidation steps examiners expect.
Consolidation.back: Steps: 1) Align accounting policies/reporting dates; 2) Eliminate investment v. subsidiary equity (share capital & pre‑acq reserves); 3) Compute goodwill/bargain; 4) Eliminate intra‑group items; 5) Compute minority interest; 6) Aggregate (AS 21).

Consolidation.front: What's the common wrong step students skip in consolidation calculations?
Consolidation.back: Error: Skipping adjustment of subsidiary’s accounting policies/reporting‑date differences before eliminating investment and computing goodwill — these adjustments must be done first (AS 21).

Consolidation.front: Minority's share of losses exceeds its interest in equity?
Consolidation.back: The excess, and further losses, are adjusted against the MAJORITY interest — unless the minority has a binding obligation to make good. Later profits go to the majority until its absorbed share is recovered.

Consolidation.front: When is a subsidiary excluded from consolidation?
Consolidation.back: Control is intended to be temporary (acquired and held exclusively for disposal in the near future), or severe long-term restrictions impair its ability to transfer funds. Account under AS 13 instead.

Consolidation.front: Subsidiary issues bonus shares — effect on cost of control?
Consolidation.back: Out of PRE-acquisition profits: no effect. Out of POST-acquisition profits: revenue profits shrink and the paid-up value held rises, so goodwill falls (or capital reserve rises).

Consolidation.front: Cumulative preference shares of the subsidiary held outside the group?
Consolidation.back: Parent computes its share of profit only AFTER deducting the subsidiary's preference dividend for the period — whether or not declared.

Branch Accounts.front: List the recognised types of branches you must distinguish in exam answers.
Branch Accounts.back: 4 types: dependent branch without full books, dependent branch with books, independent branch (full books), foreign branch — each requires different accounting treatment and presentation.

Branch Accounts.front: State the 3 ways goods are commonly invoiced to a branch and why it matters.
Branch Accounts.back: 3 methods: at cost; at invoice price (cost + markup); at selling/retail price — determines unrealised profit elimination and stock valuation in HO/branch accounts.

Branch Accounts.front: Give the formula to eliminate unrealised profit when goods sent at invoice price remain unsold at branch year‑end.
Branch Accounts.back: Unrealised profit = p/(100+p) × closing stock at invoice price (p = profit % on cost).

Branch Accounts.front: Methods of accounting for a dependent branch?
Branch Accounts.back: Debtors method (one Branch A/c — small branch); Stock and Debtors method (separate control accounts — goods at invoice price); Final Accounts method (memorandum Branch Trading and P&L); Wholesale branch method.

Branch Accounts.front: What is the headline 5‑step sequence to prepare HO’s Branch Account and adjust branch profit?
Branch Accounts.back: 5 steps: prepare memorandum trading (if needed); compute branch gross profit; adjust branch/HO expenses and remittances; prepare Branch Account in HO books; transfer branch profit/loss to HO P&L.

Branch Accounts.front: How are cash remittances and HO‑paid branch expenses treated in HO books?
Branch Accounts.back: 2 rules: Cash remittance from branch — credit Branch A/c; HO paying branch expense — debit Branch A/c (treated as advance/settlement).

Branch Accounts.front: What is the single posting students commonly forget with goods sent at invoice price?
Branch Accounts.back: Failing to eliminate unrealised profit in unsold branch stock — must adjust using p/(100+p) × stock at invoice price.

Branch Accounts.front: How are independent branches treated for preparation of final accounts?
Branch Accounts.back: Independent branch prepares full Trading, P&L and Balance Sheet; HO records branch’s net balance and treats branch as a separate accounting unit.

Branch Accounts.front: Foreign branch under AS 11 — integral vs non-integral?
Branch Accounts.back: Integral: monetary items at closing rate, non-monetary at historical rate, income/expenses at average rate, depreciation at the asset's rate; difference to P&L. Non-integral: ALL assets and liabilities at closing rate, income/expenses at average; difference to Foreign Currency Translation Reserve.

Branch Accounts.front: If a branch keeps its own debtors ledger but HO collects a debtor for the branch, what single entry does HO pass?
Branch Accounts.back: Debit Bank/Cash; Credit Branch A/c — showing collection on branch’s behalf (branch books record debtor settlement).

Branch Accounts.front: Goods or cash in transit between HO and branch at year-end?
Branch Accounts.back: Adjust in ONE set of books, usually HO: Goods-in-transit A/c Dr / Cash-in-transit A/c Dr → To Branch A/c. Shown as an asset; reversed next year.

Branch Accounts.front: Inter-branch transfer of goods — entry in HO books?
Branch Accounts.back: Receiving Branch A/c Dr → To Supplying Branch A/c. Each branch records it through its Head Office account, not through the other branch.

Branch Accounts.front: Stock and Debtors method — which accounts are opened?
Branch Accounts.back: Branch Stock A/c (at invoice price), Branch Debtors A/c, Branch Expenses A/c, Goods Sent to Branch A/c, Branch Adjustment A/c (the loading — gives gross profit), Branch P&L A/c.

Branch Accounts.front: Shortage or surplus in Branch Stock A/c kept at invoice price?
Branch Accounts.back: Split it: the LOADING part goes to Branch Adjustment A/c, the COST part to Branch P&L A/c. Normal loss: adjust only the loading.

Branch Accounts.front: Branch fixed asset account kept in HO books — depreciation entries?
Branch Accounts.back: Branch books: Depreciation A/c Dr → To Head Office A/c. HO books: Branch A/c Dr → To Branch Fixed Asset A/c. Same for an asset bought by the branch: Branch debits HO; HO debits Branch Asset.

AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.front: Under which heading must material accounting policies be presented in the financial statements?
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.back: 'Summary of significant accounting policies' — a separate note disclosing material policies used (AS 1).

AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.front: Change in accounting policy — what does AS 1 require?
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.back: Disclose any change with a material effect in the current period or later periods, and the AMOUNT of the effect to the extent ascertainable. If not ascertainable, say so. No restatement of earlier years.

AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.front: Change has no material effect this year but will in later years?
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.back: The fact of the change must still be disclosed in the period in which it is adopted (AS 1).

AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.front: How are changes in accounting estimates treated under AS 1 (vs policy changes)?
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.back: Accounted prospectively — recognize effects in current and future periods only; do not restate prior periods; disclose nature and effect if material (AS 1/AS 5 distinction).

AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.front: What must you do if you cannot quantify the effect of a change in accounting policy?
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.back: State that the effect cannot be quantified, give reasons, and disclose the nature of the change and the periods affected (AS 1).
Going concern, Consistency, Accrual. If followed — no disclosure needed. If NOT followed — the fact must be disclosed.

AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.front: Name the specific measurement bases/policy details examiners expect disclosed (give common examples).
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.back: State measurement bases: inventory valuation (FIFO/weighted average), depreciation method and rates, revenue recognition policy, investments valuation, foreign currency translation and government grants (AS 1).

AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.front: Are immaterial accounting policies required to be disclosed?
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.back: No — disclose only material policies; immaterial items may be aggregated and omission is acceptable if immaterial (AS 1).

AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.front: What guides the SELECTION of accounting policies?
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.back: Prudence (provide for known losses, do not anticipate profits), Substance over form, Materiality. Aim: a true and fair view.

AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.front: May an entity use boilerplate statements like ‘accounts prepared in accordance with AS’ instead of specifics?
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.back: No — disclose specific policies and measurement bases; avoid generic/boilerplate statements that fail to reveal key judgments or methods (AS 1).

AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.front: Does disclosing a wrong policy cure it?
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies.back: No. Disclosure of accounting policies, or of changes in them, cannot remedy a wrong or inappropriate treatment in the accounts (AS 1).

AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.back: Significant events, favourable or unfavourable, between the balance sheet date and the date the financial statements are APPROVED by the Board of Directors (or other approving authority).

AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.front: When must you adjust amounts in the financial statements for events after the balance sheet date?
AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.back: Adjust when the event provides evidence of conditions that existed at the balance sheet date (adjusting events) — revise recognised amounts accordingly (AS 4).

AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.front: Non-adjusting events — where are they disclosed?
AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.back: No change to the figures. Material changes and commitments affecting the financial position are disclosed in the REPORT OF THE APPROVING AUTHORITY (Board's report): nature of the event and an estimate of its effect, or that it cannot be estimated.

AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.front: How should a proposed final dividend declared after the balance sheet date be treated under AS 4?
AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.back: Proposed/dividend declared after the balance sheet date is non‑adjusting: do not recognise as a liability at the balance sheet date; disclose amount and that it arose after the balance sheet date (AS 4).

AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.front: If events after the balance sheet date cast doubt on going concern, what is required?
AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.back: If events show going concern assumption is no longer appropriate, change basis from going concern, adjust amounts to liquidation basis where necessary and disclose material uncertainties (AS 4).

AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.front: Name three classic adjusting events often tested under AS 4.
AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.back: Examples: settlement of a court case confirming a pre‑BS liability; customer bankruptcy confirming receivable impairment; discovery of errors or fraud indicating conditions existed at BS — adjust (AS 4).

AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.front: Name three classic non‑adjusting events commonly tested under AS 4.
AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.back: Examples: major business combination after BS; major fire/ flood destroying assets after BS; decline in market value of investments after BS — no adjustment, disclose if material (AS 4).

AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.front: Debtor becomes insolvent after the balance sheet date — adjusting or not?
AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.back: Depends on WHY. Loss caused by conditions existing at the balance sheet date (already in trouble): adjusting — provide. Caused by an event after that date (fire at his premises in April): non-adjusting — disclose.

AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.front: How do you distinguish an event that causes a change in estimate versus an adjusting event under AS 4?
AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.back: If the event provides evidence of conditions existing at the balance sheet date, treat as adjusting (revise amounts); if not, it’s a change due to post‑BS conditions and is non‑adjusting (AS 4).

AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.front: Exceptions — events after the date that are adjusted anyway?
AS 4 — Events occurring after Balance Sh.back: Where statute requires, or where the event shows the going concern assumption no longer holds (e.g. destruction of the major plant) — then the basis of accounting itself changes.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: What valuation rule must you apply to inventories at each balance-sheet date under AS 2?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Lower of cost and net realisable value — AS 2: carry inventory at lower of cost and NRV (selling price less costs to complete and to sell).

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: Which specific costs form 'cost of inventories' for manufactured goods under AS 2?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Include: direct materials, direct labour, and production overheads (variable + fixed allocated based on normal capacity) plus other costs to bring to present location/condition — AS 2.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: How must fixed production overheads be allocated to inventory according to AS 2?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Allocate fixed production overheads on the basis of normal production capacity; costs due to abnormal under‑utilisation are expensed — AS 2.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: List costs that AS 2 requires you to exclude from inventory cost.
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Exclude: abnormal wastage, storage costs (unless integral to production), non‑production administrative overheads, selling costs and interest — AS 2.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: How are abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour and production overheads treated under AS 2?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Abnormal wastage is recognised as an expense of the period; do not capitalise into inventory cost — AS 2.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: Which cost formulas does AS 2 permit for assigning costs to inventories?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Use specific identification for distinct items; otherwise FIFO or weighted average cost formula. Apply chosen formula consistently — AS 2.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: Give the AS 2 formula for Net Realisable Value (NRV).
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: NRV = estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business less estimated costs of completion and estimated costs necessary to make the sale — AS 2.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: Joint products and by-products under AS 2?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Joint costs: allocate on a rational basis, e.g. relative sales value at separation or at completion. By-products, scrap and waste: measured at NRV, and that value is DEDUCTED from the cost of the main product.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: Cost vs NRV — compared how, and how often?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Item by item (or groups of similar items) — never total cost against total NRV. Reassess NRV at every balance sheet date. Under a firm sales contract, NRV = the contract price.
The accounting policy adopted including the cost formula used; the total carrying amount of inventories and its classification (raw materials, WIP, finished goods, stores, loose tools).

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: How is the cost of inventories of purchased goods determined under AS 2?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Cost = purchase price plus import duties, transport, handling and other costs to bring to present location/condition; less trade discounts, rebates — AS 2.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: How should costs of idle capacity and similar items be treated under AS 2?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Costs of idle capacity, abnormal idle time, and non‑production overheads are expensed; they are not included in inventory cost — AS 2.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: Raw material price has fallen — do you write the raw material down?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: NOT if the finished goods will still sell at or above cost. If the finished product's NRV is below its cost, write the material down — and REPLACEMENT COST is the best measure of its NRV.

WIP under construction contracts (AS 7), WIP of service providers, shares and other financial instruments held as stock-in-trade, and producers' livestock, agricultural/forest products and mineral ores measured at NRV by trade practice.

AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.front: Standard cost and retail method — allowed?
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventory.back: Yes, for convenience, if the results approximate actual cost. Retail method: sales value less the appropriate gross margin percentage.

AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.back: Income or expense arising in the CURRENT period from ERRORS OR OMISSIONS in preparing the financial statements of one or more earlier periods. A revised estimate is not a prior period item.
Included in the current year's profit or loss, with their nature and amount disclosed separately so that the impact on current profit can be seen. Opening balances and comparatives are NOT restated.

AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.front: What is an extraordinary item, and how is it shown?
AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.back: Income or expense from events clearly distinct from ordinary activities and not expected to recur frequently — e.g. earthquake loss, attachment of property. Part of net profit, but nature and amount disclosed SEPARATELY on the face of the P&L.

AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.front: When may an accounting policy be changed (AS 5)?
AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.back: Only if required by statute, required for compliance with an Accounting Standard, or it gives a more appropriate presentation. Disclose the change and its impact; if the amount is not ascertainable, say so.

AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.front: Change in accounting estimate — how is it accounted for (AS 5)?
AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.back: Prospectively: in the P&L of the period of change, and of future periods if they are affected too. No prior period adjustment — a revised estimate is neither a prior period item nor extraordinary.

AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.front: Is restating last year's figures the fix for an error found this year?
AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.back: No. Under AS 5 the correction passes through THIS year's P&L as a prior period item, separately disclosed. Retrospective restatement is Ind AS 8, not this syllabus.

AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.front: Exceptional items (items within ordinary activities needing separate disclosure)?
AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.back: Ordinary-activity items of such size, nature or incidence that disclosure is relevant: inventory write-downs, restructuring costs, disposal of fixed assets or long-term investments, litigation settlements, reversal of provisions.

AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.front: What is NOT a change in accounting policy?
AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.back: Adopting a policy for events that differ in substance from earlier ones, or for events that did not occur before or were immaterial.

AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.front: Change in depreciation method — policy or estimate?
AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.back: A change in accounting ESTIMATE (AS 10 revised) — applied prospectively. Change in inventory cost formula (FIFO to weighted average) is a change in POLICY.

AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.front: Hard to tell whether it is a change in policy or in estimate?
AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.back: Treat it as a change in accounting estimate, with appropriate disclosure (AS 5).

AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.front: Where does the effect of a change in estimate go in the P&L?
AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period.back: In the same classification as the original estimate: ordinary if it was ordinary, extraordinary if it was extraordinary. Period of change, and future periods if they are affected.

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: Define ‘construction contract’ in exam-precise terms under AS 7.
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: A contract specifically negotiated for construction of an asset (or a closely interrelated/indivisible combination of assets) — i.e., agreement to construct, install or commission physical assets for a customer.

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: State the conditions required to apply the Percentage of Completion method.
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: 5 conditions: probable economic benefits; contract revenue measurable reliably; contract costs measurable reliably; stage of completion measurable reliably; costs to complete estimable reliably. All must be met to use percentage-of-completion.

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: How is ‘stage of completion’ normally measured? Give the standard formula and the accepted alternative.
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: Standard — cost-to-cost: stage = costs incurred to date ÷ estimated total contract costs. Alternative — physical progress (survey of work performed) only if it gives a more reliable measure.

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: Give the exact rule/formula to recognise contract revenue and recognised profit under percentage completion.
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: Revenue recognised = Contract revenue × Stage of completion. Recognised profit = Revenue recognised − Contract costs incurred to date (equivalently stage × total estimated profit, if using proportional profit method).

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: Outcome of a contract cannot be estimated reliably — what is recognised?
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: Revenue only to the extent of contract costs incurred whose recovery is PROBABLE; contract costs expensed as incurred; no profit. Expected loss still recognised at once. (AS 7 has no 'completed contract method'.)

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: When and how must an expected loss on a contract be recognised?
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: Recognise entire expected loss immediately as an expense as soon as a loss is probable, irrespective of stage of completion (no deferral under either method).

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: Contract costs — what is in, what is out?
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: In: direct costs (site labour, materials, plant depreciation, hire, design), attributable costs allocated (insurance, construction overheads, borrowing costs per AS 16), costs chargeable to the customer. Out: general administration, selling costs, unreimbursed R&D, depreciation of idle plant.

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: When are variations, claims and incentive payments included in contract revenue?
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: Include only when it is probable the customer will pay and the amount can be measured reliably; otherwise treat as contingent and disclose until recognition criteria met.

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: How to present work‑in‑progress and progress billings on the balance sheet?
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: If costs + recognised profit > progress billings → show gross amount due from customers (asset). If progress billings > costs + recognised profit → show gross amount due to customers (liability).

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: Give the immediate accounting treatment for amounts recoverable from customers and retentions.
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: Amounts recoverable recognised as receivables when probable of recovery; retentions are deducted from progress billings and shown separately (disclosed as part of receivables/contract asset until collected).

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: Cost-to-cost method — which costs are left out of 'costs incurred to date'?
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: Costs relating to FUTURE activity: materials delivered to site but not yet installed or used, and advances paid to sub-contractors for work not yet done.

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: List the key AS 7 disclosures required in each reporting period (short list for exams).
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: Disclose contract revenue recognised, method of revenue recognition and stage measurement, methods to measure contract costs, contract costs incurred, recognised profits less losses, retentions, and gross amount due from/to customers plus contingencies.

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: Expected loss on a contract — working for the provision?
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: Total expected loss = total estimated cost − contract revenue. Recognise ALL of it now: loss already reflected (cost incurred − revenue recognised) plus a provision for the balance. Stage of completion is irrelevant.

AS 7 — Construction Contracts.front: Fixed price vs cost plus contract — reliability conditions?
AS 7 — Construction Contracts.back: Fixed price: revenue, costs to complete and stage of completion all reliably measurable, benefits probable. Cost plus: benefits probable and attributable costs clearly identified and reliably measured.

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: What are the exact recognition criteria for PPE under AS 10 you must state in the exam?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: 2 criteria: probable future economic benefits and cost reliably measurable.

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: Which cost items must be included when initially measuring an item of PPE?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: 3 inclusions: purchase price; directly attributable costs; initial estimate of dismantling/restoration. Capitalise qualifying borrowing costs (AS 10; AS 16).

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: What are your permitted choices for measuring PPE after initial recognition?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: 2 models: cost model or revaluation model for subsequent measurement; apply consistently by class of asset (AS 10).

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: Revaluation increase and decrease under AS 10?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: Increase: credited to Revaluation Surplus (owners' interests) — to P&L only to the extent it reverses an earlier decrease charged there. Decrease: to P&L — except to the extent of a credit in the surplus for that asset.

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: How often must revaluations be done to meet AS 10 requirements?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: Revalue with sufficient regularity so carrying amount does not differ materially from fair value; frequency depends on market volatility (AS 10).

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: When must you use component accounting for PPE?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: 2 conditions: part’s cost is significant and it has a different useful life — account and depreciate that component separately (AS 10).

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: How often must useful life and residual value be reviewed, and how are changes applied?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: Review useful life and residual value at each balance sheet date; changes applied prospectively (AS 10).

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: Which depreciation method must you choose if exam question asks?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: Select method reflecting asset’s consumption pattern; if indeterminable, use straight-line (AS 10).

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: When can subsequent expenditure on PPE be capitalised?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: Capitalise only if expenditure brings probable future benefits and cost is measurable; routine repairs and maintenance are expensed (AS 10).

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: When is an item of PPE derecognised and what is the profit/loss treatment?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: Derecognise on disposal or when no future benefits remain; recognise gain/loss in statement of profit and loss; transfer revaluation surplus to retained earnings on disposal (AS 10).

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: How do you account for exchange/part-exchange of PPE under AS 10?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: If transaction has commercial substance, measure new asset at fair value; if not, measure at carrying amount of the old asset (AS 10).

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: What must you disclose for PPE — list the key disclosure items to memorise.
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: 7 disclosures: measurement basis; depreciation method; useful lives/rates; gross carrying & accumulated depreciation; reconciliation of carrying amount; revaluation details; restrictions and capital commitments (AS 10).

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: Costs that are NOT part of the cost of PPE?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: Opening a new facility, introducing a new product (advertising), conducting business in a new location or with new customers (staff training), administration and general overheads, initial operating losses. Income from incidental operations goes to P&L.

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: When does depreciation start and stop?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: Starts when the asset is AVAILABLE for use. Stops at the earlier of being retired from active use and held for disposal, or derecognition. It does NOT stop when the asset is idle. Land is not depreciated.

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: Revaluation — one asset or the whole class? And the surplus later?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: The ENTIRE class must be revalued. The surplus may be transferred to revenue reserves on derecognition, or gradually as the asset is used — directly, never through P&L.

AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.front: Asset retired from active use and held for disposal?
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment.back: Carry at the LOWER of carrying amount and net realisable value; recognise any write-down in P&L. Spares and stand-by equipment are PPE if they meet the definition, otherwise inventory.

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: Core conditions for recognising revenue under AS 9?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: The revenue is MEASURABLE, and at the time of sale or service it is not unreasonable to expect ULTIMATE COLLECTION. If collection is uncertain at that time, postpone recognition.

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: When is revenue from sale of goods recognised under AS 9?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: When 1) significant risks and rewards of ownership have transferred, 2) no effective control retained, and 3) measurement and collectibility are probable (AS 9).

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: Revenue from services — the two methods?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: Proportionate completion method: recognised as each act is performed, in proportion to completion. Completed service contract method: recognised when the sole or final act is done and the service is chargeable.

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: Interest, royalties and dividends — when recognised?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: Interest: time-proportion basis (amount outstanding × rate). Royalties: accrual basis as per the agreement. Dividends: when the owner's RIGHT TO RECEIVE payment is established.

Construction contracts (AS 7), hire purchase and lease agreements, government grants and subsidies, insurance contracts of insurers. Also not 'revenue': gains on sale or revaluation of fixed assets, holding gains, exchange gains.

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: Uncertainty about collection arises AFTER the sale was recognised?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: Do not reverse the revenue. Make a separate PROVISION for the uncertain amount. (If the uncertainty existed at the time of sale, recognition is postponed.)

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: Sale on approval or 'sale or return' — when is it revenue?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: When the buyer formally accepts, does an act adopting the transaction, or the time for rejection has elapsed (a reasonable time if none is fixed). Guaranteed sale with money-back: recognise at sale with a provision for returns.

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: Consignment sales and 'bill and hold' sales?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: Consignment: no revenue until the consignee sells to a third party. Bill and hold (delivery delayed at the buyer's request, buyer takes title): recognise, provided the goods are on hand, identified and ready for delivery.

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: What items are excluded from the amount of revenue recognised?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: Revenue measured at fair value of consideration, net of trade discounts, rebates and indirect taxes collected on behalf of third parties (AS 9).

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: Goods sold subject to installation and inspection?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: No revenue until the customer accepts delivery and installation and inspection are complete. If installation is simple (e.g. a TV set), recognise on delivery.

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: How is revenue accounted for in principal versus agent arrangements?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: Principal recognises gross revenue; agent recognises only net commission/fee — identify who bears significant risks and rewards to classify (AS 9).
Besides the AS 1 policy disclosure: the circumstances in which revenue recognition has been POSTPONED pending resolution of significant uncertainties.

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: Instalment sales — how is the price split?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: Sale price EXCLUDING interest is revenue on the date of sale. The interest element is recognised over time, in proportion to the unpaid balance.

AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.front: Subscriptions, advertising commission, tuition and membership fees?
AS 9 — Revenue Recognition.back: Publication subscriptions: straight-line over the period. Advertising commission: when the advertisement appears. Tuition fees: over the period of instruction. Entrance fee: generally capitalised; membership fee: over the period of the benefits.

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: How do you distinguish monetary vs non‑monetary items for AS 11 translation?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Monetary items — cash, receivables, payables; non‑monetary — inventory, PPE, goodwill. Translation rules differ: monetary = closing rate; non‑monetary = historical rate or valuation‑date rate if at fair value (AS 11).

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: Which rate is used to record a foreign currency transaction on initial recognition?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Spot rate on the transaction date — use the exchange rate at the date of the transaction to record initial recognition of the foreign currency amount (AS 11).

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: At the reporting (balance sheet) date, which rate must be used for monetary items?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Closing rate at the balance sheet date — translate all monetary assets and liabilities at the closing (balance sheet) exchange rate (AS 11).

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: How are non‑monetary items carried at historical cost translated at reporting date?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Historical rate — translate non‑monetary items measured at historical cost using the exchange rate prevailing on the date of the original transaction (AS 11).

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: How are non‑monetary items carried at fair value translated?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Valuation‑date rate — translate non‑monetary items measured at fair value using the exchange rate on the date when the fair value was determined (AS 11).

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: Which exchange differences are recognised in profit or loss?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Exchange differences on settlement or on translation of monetary items — recognised in profit or loss in the period in which they arise (AS 11).

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: Integral vs non-integral foreign operation — translation rules?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Integral: as if the transactions were the enterprise's own — monetary at closing rate, non-monetary at historical rate, differences to P&L. Non-integral: all assets and liabilities at closing rate, income/expenses at transaction (average) rates, differences to Foreign Currency Translation Reserve.

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: Where are translation differences recorded, and when are they recycled to profit or loss?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Separate component of equity — cumulative translation differences are recognised in a Foreign Currency Translation Reserve; on disposal of the foreign operation the cumulative amount is recognised in profit or loss (AS 11).

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: How are exchange differences on long‑term monetary items that form part of a net investment in a foreign operation treated?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Recorded in equity — exchange differences on monetary items forming part of a net investment in a foreign operation are recognised in the Foreign Currency Translation Reserve, not in profit or loss (AS 11).

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: When is it permissible to use an average exchange rate to translate income and expenses?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Average rate for the period may be used when exchange rates do not fluctuate significantly and the average reasonably approximates actual transaction rates; otherwise use transaction‑date rates (AS 11).

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: Forward exchange contract NOT for trading or speculation?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Premium or discount at inception is amortised as expense/income over the life of the contract. Exchange differences recognised in P&L in the period the rates change. Profit or loss on cancellation or renewal: P&L of that period.

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: Forward contract held for trading or speculation?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Ignore the premium or discount. Mark to market at each balance sheet date: gain or loss = forward rate available for the remaining maturity vs the contracted rate. To P&L.

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: Para 46/46A option for long-term foreign currency monetary items?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Exchange differences may be: added to or deducted from the cost of a DEPRECIABLE capital asset and depreciated over its remaining life; otherwise accumulated in FCMITDA and amortised over the life of the item. Irrevocable once chosen.

AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.front: Foreign operation reclassified between integral and non-integral?
AS 11 — The Effects of Changes in Foreig.back: Apply the new translation procedure prospectively from the date of change. Integral → non-integral: differences on non-monetary assets go to FCTR. Non-integral → integral: FCTR stays until disposal.

AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.front: When is a government grant recognised in the books?
AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.back: Recognition: when there is reasonable assurance that the entity will comply with conditions and the grant will be received (AS 12).

AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.front: What are the permitted treatments for a grant related to a depreciable asset?
AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.back: Two options: (a) deduct grant from asset carrying amount and depreciate net; or (b) record as deferred income and amortise to P&L over asset's useful life (AS 12).

AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.front: How must grants related to revenue (compensation for expenses) be recognised?
AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.back: Matching: recognise in profit & loss over periods in which related expenses are incurred; present either by deducting related expense or as separate other income (AS 12).

AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.front: Non-monetary government grants — at what value?
AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.back: Given at a CONCESSIONAL rate: record at acquisition cost. Given FREE: record at a nominal value. (Fair value is IAS 20, not AS 12.)

Extraordinary item (AS 5). Revenue grant: first against unamortised deferred credit, balance to P&L. Asset grant: increase the asset's book value (depreciate prospectively over remaining life) or reduce deferred income. Promoters' contribution: reduce capital reserve.

AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.front: Grant in the nature of promoters' contribution?
AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.back: Given with reference to total investment or towards total capital outlay, with no repayment expected: credit to CAPITAL RESERVE as part of shareholders' funds. Not distributable as dividend, not deferred income.

AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.front: What minimum disclosures does AS 12 require about government grants?
AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.back: Disclosures: accounting policy, nature and extent of grants recognised, unfulfilled conditions/contingencies, and any repayable grants (AS 12).

AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.front: If you deduct a grant from an asset, what is the depreciation basis?
AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.back: Depreciation: charge depreciation on the asset's carrying amount after deducting the grant, over the asset's remaining useful life (AS 12).

AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.front: If you recognise a grant as deferred income, how should it be amortised?
AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.back: Amortisation: allocate deferred grant to income on a systematic basis over the useful life of the related asset, generally on same basis as depreciation (AS 12).

AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.front: Grant received as compensation for past losses, or as immediate support with no further costs?
AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.back: Recognise in P&L in the period it becomes RECEIVABLE — as an extraordinary item if appropriate (AS 5).

AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.front: Grant for a NON-depreciable asset, and a grant equal to the whole cost?
AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants.back: Non-depreciable asset (land): credit to capital reserve; if conditions require spending, credit to income over the period those costs are charged. Grant = whole cost of the asset: show the asset at a nominal value.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: What do 'borrowing costs' include under AS 16?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: Interest and commitment charges; amortisation of discounts or premiums; amortisation of ancillary costs of arranging borrowings; finance charges under finance leases; exchange differences on foreign currency borrowings to the extent they are an adjustment to interest cost.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: What is a qualifying asset — and how long is 'substantial'?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: An asset that necessarily takes a substantial period to get ready for its intended use or sale. Ordinarily TWELVE MONTHS is substantial, unless a shorter or longer period can be justified on the facts.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: When does capitalization of borrowing costs commence? Give the three required conditions.
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: 3 conditions: expenditures for the asset incurred; borrowing costs incurred; activities to prepare the asset for use are in progress. All three must be met.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: When is capitalisation suspended — and when not?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: Suspended during extended periods in which ACTIVE DEVELOPMENT is interrupted. Not suspended while substantial technical and administrative work continues, or when a temporary delay is a necessary part of the process (high water levels while building a bridge).

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: When does capitalization cease? How about parts of an asset?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: Cease when substantially all activities to prepare asset are complete. If parts are ready earlier, cease capitalization for those parts.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: How are borrowing costs treated for funds borrowed specifically for a qualifying asset?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: Capitalise actual borrowing costs incurred on the specific borrowings less any investment income on temporarily invested borrowed funds.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: General borrowings — amount to capitalise, and the ceiling?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: Capitalisation rate (weighted average cost of general borrowings outstanding) × expenditure on the qualifying asset. The amount capitalised can NEVER exceed the borrowing costs actually incurred in the period.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: How is the weighted average borrowing rate determined?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: Weighted average = borrowing costs of general borrowings divided by outstanding general borrowings during the period; exclude borrowings specifically for qualifying assets.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: What borrowing costs are not capitalised and must be expensed?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: Borrowing costs not directly attributable to qualifying assets are expensed; costs after completion or before commencement are recognised as expense.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: Order the calculation steps when both specific and general borrowings finance a qualifying asset.
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: 4 steps: 1) identify qualifying expenditures; 2) apply specific-borrowing actual cost (net investment income); 3) compute weighted average rate for general borrowings; 4) apply it to remaining expenditures.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: How are funds temporarily invested treated when specific borrowings exist?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: Income from temporary investment of specifically borrowed funds is deducted from borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: What minimum disclosures does AS 16 require about borrowing costs?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: 3 disclosures: amount of borrowing costs capitalised during period; capitalization rate used for general borrowings; amount of borrowing costs recognised as expense and accounting policy.

AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.front: Exchange difference on a foreign currency loan — how much is 'borrowing cost'?
AS 16 — Borrowing Costs.back: Only up to the difference between interest on an equivalent LOCAL currency borrowing and the interest on the foreign currency borrowing. Any exchange loss beyond that is an AS 11 exchange difference.

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: Within AS 15, how long must a benefit be expected to be settled for it to be classified as a short‑term employee benefit?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: 12 months: benefits expected to be settled wholly within 12 months of service rendered are short‑term employee benefits (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: How are accumulating versus non‑accumulating compensated absences recognised under AS 15?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: Full amount: accumulating compensated absences — recognise liability for full amount attributable to service to balance sheet date; non‑accumulating — recognise expense only when absence occurs (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: What is the employer’s accounting rule for defined contribution plans?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: Expense in period: employer’s obligation limited to agreed contributions; recognise contribution as expense when employee renders service; unpaid contributions shown as liability (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: Which actuarial method and discount basis does AS 15 require for measuring Defined Benefit Obligation (DBO)?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: Projected unit credit: measure DBO using projected unit credit method; discount at market yields on government bonds or equivalent at balance sheet date (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: When and how are actuarial gains and losses recognised under AS 15?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: Immediate: actuarial gains and losses are recognised immediately in profit or loss for the period in which they arise (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: How are interest cost and return on plan assets computed and presented?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: Interest / return: interest cost = opening DBO × discount rate; expected return = opening plan assets × expected rate; both recognised in profit or loss (net effect presented) (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: How is past service cost recognised when a plan is amended or curtailed?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: Past service cost: recognise immediately when benefits vest; if benefits vest in future, spread past service cost over the vesting period (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: Termination benefits under AS 15 — when recognised?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: As a liability and expense when, and only when: there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow is probable, and a reliable estimate can be made. ('Demonstrably committed' is the IAS 19 wording.)

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: How much of a plan surplus can an employer recognise as an asset under AS 15?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: Recoverable limit: recognise surplus only to the extent recoverable as present value of refunds or reduced future contributions; any excess not recognised (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: What minimum disclosures does AS 15 require for defined benefit plans?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: Reconciliation: disclose opening/closing DBO and plan assets, P&L components (service cost, interest, return, actuarial gains/losses, past service), principal actuarial assumptions, and next‑year employer contribution estimate (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: How are accumulating compensated absences treated when their settlement is expected after 12 months?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: Regardless of timing: accumulating compensated absences are recognised for the full amount attributable to service to balance‑sheet date even if settlement occurs after 12 months (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: What is the formula (order of components) for net defined benefit cost in the profit and loss?
AS 15 — Employee Benefits.back: Net defined benefit cost = current service cost + past service cost + interest cost − expected return on plan assets + actuarial gains/(losses) ± settlements; recognise in profit or loss (AS 15).

AS 15 — Employee Benefits.front: Defined contribution vs defined benefit — who carries the risk?
